idiom_name: destructuring projection; JSON.stringify key whitelist; lodash _.pick
implementation_notes: The projection is an expression, not an object: destructuring builds the narrow view (const { id, reference } = order) or drops by exclusion with a rest element ({ internalNotes, audits, ...view } = order), and when the payload is serialized immediately JSON.stringify(value, [keys]) filters keys during serialization; lodash's _.pick handles a key set that is only known at runtime. What replaces the classic filter object is a pure function - often with no class, no registration and no framework - which is why the pattern is idiomatic here rather than a structure. A hand-written recursive filter is still justified when the retained fields sit at fixed paths inside a nested tree (the flattening case), where chained destructuring stops being readable.
pitfalls: delete order.internalNotes mutates the caller's object, so every other consumer of the same message loses the field - always build a new object instead of mutating the source.

JSON.stringify's replacer array filters keys at every nesting level, so it cannot express 'keep id at the root but not inside lines', and a replacer function that returns the value unchanged silently bypasses the whitelist.
Destructuring copies references: nested objects and arrays are shared with the source, so a downstream mutation of the 'filtered' view still corrupts the original message.

A projection that only exists inside a serializer (toJSON on the domain class) runs whenever anything serializes the object - including logs and error reporting - which hides fields from places that legitimately need them.
